title: Clean vector architecture
description: White background, precise connectors, flat service symbols and crisp labels.
prompt:
Use case: scientific-educational. Asset type: courseware diagram STYLE SAMPLE for user selection. Generate one beautiful finished diagram, landscape 1536 x 1024 or wider (width strictly greater than height). All text large and readable. All labels in English. No watermark or logos. This is ONE diagram, not a comparison collage. Include a small top-left label "Option 1" and small top-right style label "Clean vector architecture".
Style: Clean flat vector-style cloud architecture illustration on pure white. Straight precise connectors, carefully aligned rectangular groups, subtle rounded cards, bold crisp dark typography, restrained blue and teal accents. Flat 2D educational architecture, no handwriting, no 3D, generous space.
Technical content, preserve exactly: Diagram title: "GCP PCA: Resilient Multi-Region Architecture". Show Users -> Global external Application Load Balancer with "Health checks". The load balancer sends requests to TWO separate region groups: "Region A" and "Region B". In EACH region a "Regional managed instance group" spans "Zone 1", "Zone 2", "Zone 3"; each zone contains one small compute icon. Both regional compute groups connect to ONE shared logical database labeled "Spanner multi-region" with sublabel "Synchronous replication". The Spanner box represents a distributed service, not a single zonal machine. Keep directional request arrows explicit. Bottom three concise learning callouts, verbatim: "Zones: isolate zone failures", "Regions: isolate region failures", "Test failover against RTO and RPO". Do not add Cloud SQL, invented SLA numbers, specific region names or guaranteed recovery times.
Use a coherent left-to-right composition and distinguish flow 1 from flow 2 where applicable. Label every arrow only when needed; minimize crossings. Maintain the same technical content as the other style samples for fair comparison. Do not add extra architecture or facts.
